title: Linked List Cycle
approach_name: Floyd slow and fast pointers
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle, without modifying the list.
Idea: Move slow one node at a time and fast two nodes at a time. If they ever reference the same node, a cycle exists; if fast reaches null, the list is acyclic.
Technique and why it applies: Inside a cycle, the faster pointer gains one node per iteration on the slower pointer, so they must eventually meet.
Invariant: If the list has no cycle, fast eventually reaches the end; a meeting can only occur when nodes repeat in a cycle.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node acyclic lists return false. Compare node identity, not node values.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Both pointers advance at fixed speeds without storing visited nodes.

title: Linked List Cycle II
approach_name: Find meeting point then cycle entrance
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the exact node where a linked-list cycle begins, or null if the list has no cycle. Do not modify the list.
Idea: First use Floyd's slow/fast pointers to find a meeting inside the cycle. If they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; their next meeting is the cycle entrance.
Technique and why it applies: The distance relationship between the head-to-entry prefix and the cycle's remaining distance makes the reset pointers meet at the entry.
Invariant: The first phase establishes that a cycle exists; the second phase converges on its first node.
Edge cases: An acyclic list returns null. A cycle may begin at the head, and a one-node self-cycle is valid.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Floyd's meeting and entrance phases use only two pointers.

title: Reorder List
approach_name: Split, reverse second half, and weave
notes:
Task and constraints: Reorder a list L0,L1,...,Ln as L0,Ln,L1,Ln-1,... without changing node values.
Idea: Find the midpoint with slow/fast pointers, detach and reverse the second half, then alternate nodes from the first and reversed second halves.
Technique and why it applies: The reversed second half places the original final node first, allowing a simple alternating merge to produce the required order.
Invariant: During weaving, the first list holds the next front node and the reversed list holds the next back node to insert.
Edge cases: Lists of length one or two need no special reordering. Detach the halves before reversing to avoid cycles.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Midpoint search, reversal, and weaving each traverse a linear portion of the list.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        if not head or not head.next:return
        slow=fast=head
        while fast.next and fast.next.next:slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next.next
        cur=slow.next;slow.next=None;prev=None
        while cur:nxt=cur.next;cur.next=prev;prev=cur;cur=nxt
        first,second=head,prev
        while second:
            a,b=first.next,second.next;first.next=second;second.next=a;first=a;second=b

title: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
approach_name: Iterative root-left-right stack
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the preorder traversal of a binary tree: visit the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree.
Idea: Use a stack. Pop and record a node, push its right child first, then its left child so the left child is processed next.
Technique and why it applies: A LIFO stack reverses push order, allowing the iterative traversal to match root-left-right recursion.
Invariant: The output is the preorder prefix already visited, and the stack holds pending subtrees in reverse processing order.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns an empty list. Push right before left to preserve the required order.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) to O(n), depending on tree shape.
complexity_reason: Every node is pushed and popped once.

approach_name: Reverse root-right-left order

Task and constraints: Return the postorder traversal of a binary tree: left subtree, right subtree, then node.
Idea: Perform an iterative root-right-left traversal by pushing left before right, collect values, then reverse the collected sequence.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing root-right-left yields left-right-root, exactly the postorder order.
Invariant: Before reversal, the collected list follows root-right-left; after reversal, it follows left-right-root.
Edge cases: Empty trees return an empty list. The method uses an explicit stack rather than recursive calls.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the stack and output list.
complexity_reason: The stack and collected traversal each store up to n nodes/values.

title: LRU Cache
approach_name: Ordered map with least-recent item first
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement LRUCache get and put with O(1) average operations and evict the least recently used key when capacity is exceeded.
Idea: __init__ stores capacity and an OrderedDict named data. get returns -1 for a missing key; otherwise move_to_end marks it recent and returns its value. put moves an existing key to the end, assigns the value, then popitem(last=False) removes the oldest item if the size exceeds capacity.
Technique and why it applies: OrderedDict maintains recency order alongside key lookup, so moving and removing entries does not require scanning all cached keys.
Invariant: data is ordered from least recently used at the front to most recently used at the end after each completed operation.
Edge cases: A missing key returns -1 without changing order. Updating an existing key refreshes its recency instead of creating a duplicate. Inserting beyond capacity removes exactly the front item; capacity zero would immediately evict each inserted item.
Complexity: get and put are O(1) average per operation; storage is O(capacity) for the OrderedDict entries.
complexity_reason: Each get and put performs a constant number of OrderedDict operations, and data stores at most capacity entries.

title: LRU Cache
approach_name: Ordered map with least-recent item first
notes:
Task and constraints: Provide LRUCache lookups and updates in O(1) average time, discarding the least recently used entry once the configured capacity is crossed.
Idea: The constructor enables access order in LinkedHashMap with super(capacity,0.75f,true). get delegates to getOrDefault, put calls super.put, and removeEldestEntry returns true when size() exceeds capacity.
Technique and why it applies: Access-ordered LinkedHashMap combines hash lookup with a linked recency order; its eviction hook removes the eldest entry automatically after insertion.
Invariant: After each public operation, the map's linked order runs from least recently accessed to most recently accessed, and size does not exceed capacity after put completes.
Edge cases: A missing key returns -1. Reading an existing key updates its access position because accessOrder is true. A new insertion beyond capacity triggers removeEldestEntry; Java's map still uses the usual integer key equality.
Complexity: get and put are O(1) average; space is O(capacity) for the map and linked entries.
complexity_reason: LinkedHashMap performs average constant-time lookup and update while retaining one linked entry per cached key.

title: Insertion Sort List
approach_name: Insert each node into sorted prefix
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort a singly linked list in ascending order using insertion sort.
Idea: Maintain a sorted list behind a dummy head. Remove each node from the input and insert it after the last sorted node whose value is less than or equal to it; if that shortcut fails, search from the dummy head.
Technique and why it applies: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each next element into its correct position.
Invariant: The nodes before the unsorted pointer form a sorted list containing exactly the nodes already processed.
Edge cases: Duplicate values are handled by inserting after existing equals. Empty and one-node lists are already sorted.
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(n^2). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each node is inserted into the sorted prefix using only pointer updates.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def insertionSortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy=ListNode(0);cur=head;tail=dummy
        while cur:
            nxt=cur.next
            if tail is dummy or tail.val<=cur.val:prev=tail
            else:
                prev=dummy
                while prev.next and prev.next.val<=cur.val:prev=prev.next
            cur.next=prev.next;prev.next=cur
            if cur.val>=tail.val if tail is not dummy else True:tail=cur
            cur=nxt
        return dummy.next

title: Sort List
approach_name: Merge sort linked list
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort a linked list in ascending order in O(n log n) time.
Idea: Split the list into halves using slow/fast pointers, recursively sort each half, and merge the two sorted lists with a dummy head.
Technique and why it applies: Merge sort works well on linked lists because splitting and merging need only sequential pointer traversal, not random access.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns a sorted list containing exactly the nodes from its input segment.
Edge cases: Empty and single-node lists are already sorted. Break the list at the midpoint before recursive calls.
Complexity: Time is O(n log n). Extra space is O(log n) for recursive calls.
complexity_reason: Each merge level processes all n nodes and there are logarithmically many levels.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next:return head
        slow,fast=head,head.next
        while fast and fast.next:slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next.next
        mid=slow.next;slow.next=None
        a=self.sortList(head);b=self.sortList(mid)
        dummy=ListNode(0);tail=dummy
        while a and b:
            if a.val<=b.val:tail.next=a;a=a.next
            else:tail.next=b;b=b.next
            tail=tail.next
        tail.next=a or b
        return dummy.next

title: Max Points on a Line
approach_name: Normalize slopes per anchor point
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of points that lie on one straight line. Coordinates may repeat, and duplicate points must be counted.
Idea: For each anchor point, count other points by normalized slope. Divide the coordinate difference by its greatest common divisor and normalize the sign so equal lines share one key; count duplicates separately.
Technique and why it applies: Every line through a fixed anchor is uniquely identified by its reduced slope, with special handling for coincident points.
Invariant: The largest slope bucket plus duplicates and the anchor is the largest collinear set through that anchor.
Edge cases: Vertical and horizontal lines need canonical slope keys. Duplicate coordinates have zero difference and must not be divided by gcd zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) expected. Extra space is O(n) per anchor.
complexity_reason: Each anchor compares against all later points and stores reduced slopes.
code:
from typing import List
from math import gcd

class Solution:
    def maxPoints(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n=len(points)
        if n<=2:return n
        best=0
        for i in range(n):
            slopes={};duplicates=0;local=0
            for j in range(i+1,n):
                dx=points[j][0]-points[i][0];dy=points[j][1]-points[i][1]
                if dx==0 and dy==0:duplicates+=1;continue
                g=gcd(dx,dy);dx//=g;dy//=g
                if dx<0:dx=-dx;dy=-dy
                elif dx==0:dy=1
                key=(dy,dx);slopes[key]=slopes.get(key,0)+1;local=max(local,slopes[key])
            best=max(best,local+duplicates+1)
        return best

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
approach_name: Evaluate operators with an operand stack
notes:
Task and constraints: Evaluate a valid reverse Polish notation expression containing integer operands and binary operators +, -, *, and /; division truncates toward zero.
Idea: Push operands. When an operator appears, pop the right operand then the left operand, apply the operator in that order, and push the result.
Technique and why it applies: In postfix notation, each operator follows its operands, so a stack holds the values waiting for an operation.
Invariant: After processing a token prefix, the stack contains the intermediate values represented by that prefix.
Edge cases: Subtraction and division are not commutative, so operand order matters. Python must implement truncation toward zero without floating-point conversion.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the operand stack.
complexity_reason: Each token is pushed or popped a constant number of times.

title: Reverse Words in a String
approach_name: Split and reverse non-empty words
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse word order while trimming surrounding whitespace and collapsing runs of spaces to one separator.
Idea: reverseWords calls s.split(), which discards leading and trailing whitespace and splits on whitespace runs, then reversed() iterates the resulting words backward and join inserts one ordinary space between them.
Technique and why it applies: Tokenization followed by reversal separates word boundaries from spacing, so the output can be rebuilt without preserving unwanted input spaces.
Invariant: At each step of the reversed iterator, the next output token is the next word from the original sentence in right-to-left order.
Edge cases: Leading and trailing spaces disappear during split. Multiple spaces between words produce a single output space. An all-whitespace string would yield no tokens and join to the empty string, although the stated examples contain words.
Complexity: Time is O(n) to split, reverse the word sequence, and join the characters; space is O(n) for the token list and result.
complexity_reason: split scans the n-character string and join materializes the reversed token sequence into a new string.

title: Reverse Words in a String
approach_name: Split and reverse non-empty words
notes:
Task and constraints: Return words in reverse order, trimming leading and trailing spaces and replacing repeated whitespace separators with one space.
Idea: reverseWords trims s, splits the remainder on the regex for one or more whitespace characters, and walks array a from its last index to zero. It appends nonempty tokens to StringBuilder out, inserting a space only after output has begun.
Technique and why it applies: Splitting into tokens isolates the words, and a reverse array traversal reconstructs their order without manually moving characters.
Invariant: Before each iteration, out contains the processed suffix of a in reverse word order, with exactly one separator between appended words.
Edge cases: Input with leading/trailing spaces is normalized by trim. The explicit one-empty-token check returns an empty string for blank input. Skipping empty tokens also avoids adding extra spaces if split produces an empty element; regex splitting handles repeated whitespace.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for trim, split, and the reverse traversal; space is O(n) for array a and StringBuilder out.
complexity_reason: The implementation scans and copies characters during trim and split, then appends each token once to out.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
approach_name: Track maximum and minimum ending products
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest product of any non-empty contiguous subarray; negative values can turn a small negative product into a large positive one.
Idea: Initialize hi, lo, and ans from nums[0]. For each later x, swap hi and lo when x is negative, update hi with max(x,hi*x), update lo with min(x,lo*x), and keep ans as the largest hi seen.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking both maximum and minimum products ending at the current index handles sign flips caused by multiplying by a negative number.
Invariant: hi and lo are respectively the maximum and minimum products of subarrays ending at the current position, so either can become the next maximum after a negative x.
Edge cases: A one-element nums list returns that element. Zero resets both ending products to zero when processed. For [-2,0,-1], ans reaches zero rather than incorrectly choosing a product across the zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each element after nums[0] is processed once; auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop visits nums[1:] once and updates only hi, lo, ans, and the current value x.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
approach_name: Track maximum and minimum ending products
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum product over all non-empty contiguous subarrays, including arrays containing zero and negative integers.
Idea: maxProduct seeds hi, lo, and ans with nums[0]. Each iteration reads x; when x is negative it swaps hi and lo through temporary int t, then uses Math.max and Math.min to update ending products and Math.max to update ans.
Technique and why it applies: The paired max/min dynamic states preserve both sign possibilities; multiplying the prior minimum by a negative x may create the new maximum.
Invariant: After processing nums[i], hi and lo describe the extreme products of subarrays ending at i, while ans stores the best product seen at any endpoint.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns nums[0]. A zero can become the best answer and breaks products spanning that position. The Java int multiplications follow 32-bit signed arithmetic, so the problem's numeric constraints must keep expected products in range.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1), with a fixed number of integer variables per array element.
complexity_reason: Each array index is visited once and all state updates use a fixed number of int variables.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
approach_name: Compare midpoint to right endpoint
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum value in a nonempty ascending array rotated at an unknown pivot; all values are distinct.
Idea: findMin sets l and r to the array endpoints. While l < r, it computes m; if nums[m] exceeds nums[r], the minimum lies to the right so l becomes m+1, otherwise r becomes m. It returns nums[l].
Technique and why it applies: Binary search discards the half that cannot contain the rotation's minimum by comparing the midpoint with the right endpoint.
Invariant: The minimum remains inside the inclusive interval nums[l:r+1] after every update.
Edge cases: An unrotated array such as [11,13,15,17] repeatedly moves r toward the first element. For [3,4,5,1,2], nums[m] > nums[r] moves l rightward. A single-element array skips the loop and returns its only value.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) because the search interval shrinks by about half each round; space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each iteration compares nums[m] with nums[r] and removes roughly half the remaining candidate interval.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
approach_name: Compare midpoint to right endpoint
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum of a nonempty rotated ascending int array whose elements are distinct.
Idea: findMin initializes l=0 and r=nums.length-1. It calculates m as l+(r-l)/2 to avoid adding the two endpoints, then moves l to m+1 if nums[m] > nums[r], or moves r to m otherwise. The converged index is returned.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search uses the sorted portions revealed by the midpoint/right comparison to retain only the half that can contain the rotation pivot.
Invariant: The minimum's index always remains within [l,r], and each branch strictly shortens this inclusive range unless it has already converged.
Edge cases: An already sorted array returns index zero. In [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], the comparison sends l past the high-valued prefix. For length one, l equals r immediately; midpoint arithmetic avoids overflow from l+r.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) and extra space is O(1), since only two bounds and a midpoint are stored.
complexity_reason: The while loop halves the candidate range and uses only l, r, and m as index variables.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
approach_name: Shrink equal right endpoint
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicate values; duplicates make some midpoint comparisons ambiguous.
Idea: findMin keeps bounds l and r and compares nums[m] with nums[r]. A smaller midpoint moves r to m, a larger midpoint moves l to m+1, and equality decrements r by one before the loop repeats.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search handles decisive comparisons logarithmically, while shrinking an equal right endpoint safely removes one duplicate candidate when ordering cannot identify a side.
Invariant: At least one occurrence of the minimum remains within nums[l:r+1] after each branch.
Edge cases: [1,3,5] returns 1 without rotation. [2,2,2,0,1] narrows around the zero. An all-equal array may only shrink r one step at a time, so duplicates cause O(n) worst-case behavior.
Complexity: Typical time is O(log n), worst-case time is O(n) when equal values force single-step shrinkage; space is O(1).
time_complexity: O(log n) typical, O(n) worst case
complexity_reason: The bounds shrink each iteration, but repeated equality may decrement r only once per pass.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
approach_name: Shrink equal right endpoint
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest value in a rotated ascending int array where equal values may occur.
Idea: findMin calculates m between l and r. If nums[m] is smaller than nums[r], it keeps the left half through m; if larger, it advances l past m; if equal, it decrements r by one because the comparison is inconclusive.
Technique and why it applies: The binary-search branches exploit strict ordering, and the equality branch removes only a redundant rightmost candidate to avoid discarding a possible minimum.
Invariant: The inclusive interval from l to r still contains a minimum after each branch, including the one-element decrement on equality.
Edge cases: [1,3,5] converges to 1. [2,2,2,0,1] eventually discards duplicate 2s and reaches 0. If every value is equal, the r-- branch dominates and the search takes linear time; int indices remain within the array bounds.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) in typical cases and O(n) worst case with duplicates; space is O(1).
time_complexity: O(log n) typical, O(n) worst case
complexity_reason: Each loop iteration changes l or r, and repeated equal endpoints can require up to n decrements.

title: Min Stack
approach_name: Store each value with prefix minimum
notes:
Task and constraints: Design a stack whose push, pop, top, and getMin operations each take O(1) time.
Idea: MinStack stores pairs in stack. push appends (val, min(val, previous minimum)), using val itself when the stack is empty. pop removes the last pair; top reads its value and getMin reads the pair's stored minimum.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-minimum augmentation saves the minimum at every stack depth, avoiding a scan of all stored values when getMin is called.
Invariant: The second component of stack[-1] is the smallest value among all entries currently in the stack.
Edge cases: The first push stores the same value in both tuple fields. Pushing a smaller value makes it the new minimum, and popping it exposes the earlier minimum stored below. Calling pop, top, or getMin on an empty stack would raise an indexing/pop error; valid operation sequences must avoid that.
Complexity: Each operation is O(1); space is O(n) for one value/minimum pair per pushed element.
complexity_reason: push reads only the last tuple and appends one pair; top and getMin access stack[-1] directly.

title: Min Stack
approach_name: Store each value with prefix minimum
notes:
Task and constraints: Support constant-time stack push, pop, top, and getMin operations by keeping enough information to restore the minimum after a pop.
Idea: MinStack uses Deque<int[]> st. push places a two-element array containing val and either val or the previous top pair's minimum. pop removes that pair; top returns element zero and getMin returns element one from st.peek().
Technique and why it applies: Storing a prefix minimum beside each value makes the current minimum available at the deque head without traversing earlier entries.
Invariant: For every pair on st, its second integer is the minimum of the values from the bottom through that pair's stack depth.
Edge cases: The first push stores val in both positions. If a smaller number is pushed, getMin returns it; after pop, the previous pair restores the older minimum. ArrayDeque rejects null elements, but each push creates a non-null int array; empty-stack calls are not guarded.
Complexity: All four operations take O(1) time; space is O(n) for the deque entries and their two-int arrays.
complexity_reason: Each method performs a constant number of deque operations and stores one two-integer array per push.

title: Binary Tree Upside Down
approach_name: Rewire while descending the left spine
notes:
Task and constraints: Flip a binary tree with the stated shape so its leftmost node becomes root and each parent is rewired below its original left child.
Idea: upsideDownBinaryTree returns root when it is absent or has no left child. Otherwise it recursively flips root.left into new_root, assigns the original right child to root.left.left and root to root.left.right, clears root's two child links, then returns new_root.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive left-spine traversal reaches the future root first, then rewires each ancestor while recursion unwinds.
Invariant: After the recursive call, new_root is the flipped subtree rooted at the original left child, while root's original child pointers are still available for the two reassignment steps.
Edge cases: A null root returns null. A single node or a node without a left child is already the result. The right child is moved to the new left link and must be saved before root.right is cleared; recursion depth follows the left spine.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each node on the left spine is visited once; auxiliary space is O(h) for recursion depth h.
complexity_reason: The recursive call follows root.left once per level and performs constant pointer updates while unwinding.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def upsideDownBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        if not root or not root.left:return root
        new_root=self.upsideDownBinaryTree(root.left)
        root.left.left=root.right;root.left.right=root
        root.left=None;root.right=None
        return new_root

title: Binary Tree Upside Down
approach_name: Rewire while descending the left spine
notes:
Task and constraints: Transform a specially shaped binary tree so the original leftmost node becomes the root and old parent-child links are rotated.
Idea: upsideDownBinaryTree stops at null or when root.left is null. It recursively obtains newRoot from root.left, assigns root.right to root.left.left and root to root.left.right, clears root.left and root.right, and returns newRoot.
Technique and why it applies: The recursion descends the left spine before changing links, allowing each parent to become the right child of its original left child during unwinding.
Invariant: At each return, newRoot points to the final root of the already transformed lower subtree; the current root is then attached beneath its former left child.
Edge cases: A null root remains null. A leaf is returned unchanged. For a node with left and right children, the right child becomes the new left child of the old left node; the problem's shape guarantee is needed for valid rewiring. Java recursion uses O(h) stack frames.
Complexity: Time is O(n) over the visited nodes and auxiliary space is O(h) for the recursive call stack.
complexity_reason: The method follows root.left recursively and executes a fixed number of TreeNode pointer assignments at each level.

title: Read N Characters Given Read4
approach_name: Repeatedly read chunks until n or EOF
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement read(buf,n) using read4, copying at most n available characters into buf and returning the number copied; this implementation assumes a single call.
Idea: read creates a four-character tmp buffer and tracks total. While total<n, it calls read4, stops on EOF, copies min(count,n-total) characters, and stops early when read4 returns fewer than four characters.
Technique and why it applies: Chunked reading uses the provided four-character API while limiting each copy to the remaining requested count.
Invariant: buf[0:total] contains exactly the characters copied so far, and total never exceeds n.
Edge cases: n=0 skips the loop and returns zero. read4 returning zero ends at EOF without copying. If n is smaller than count, take limits the copy; a short chunk signals the source has reached its end.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for copying at most n requested characters; extra space is O(1) for tmp, which always has four slots.
complexity_reason: The loop copies at most n characters into buf and reuses a fixed four-slot temporary list.
code:
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def read(self, buf: List[str], n: int) -> int:
        total=0;tmp=['']*4
        while total<n:
            count=read4(tmp)
            if count==0:break
            take=min(count,n-total)
            for i in range(take):buf[total+i]=tmp[i]
            total+=take
            if count<4:break
        return total

title: Read N Characters Given Read4
approach_name: Repeatedly read chunks until n or EOF
notes:
Task and constraints: Read no more than n characters from the judge-provided read4 API into buf, returning the count copied in this single call.
Idea: read allocates char[] tmp of length four, calls read4 while total<n, and stops when count is zero. It computes take as the smaller of count and remaining capacity, copies with System.arraycopy, advances total, and breaks when count<4.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-size chunk buffering matches the API contract; limiting take prevents the final chunk from writing past the n-character request.
Invariant: The valid output prefix is buf[0..total), and total advances only by the number of characters copied into that prefix.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero without calling read4. A zero count signals EOF. If read4 returns four characters but only one slot remains, take copies just one; a short chunk ends the loop after its available characters are copied.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for at most n copied characters; extra space is O(1) for the four-character tmp array.
complexity_reason: System.arraycopy copies at most the remaining request size, and tmp always contains four char slots.

title: Read N Characters Given Read4 II - Call multiple times
approach_name: Keep unread characters between calls
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement read(buf,n) across repeated calls while preserving characters read in advance but not yet delivered to a caller.
Idea: __init__ stores _buf4, _i, and _size. read refills the four-character buffer only when _i equals _size, resets _i, stops if read4 returns zero, and otherwise copies one character at a time into buf until total reaches n.
Technique and why it applies: A persistent chunk buffer carries unread characters between calls, avoiding loss when one read4 fetch returns more data than the current request needs.
Invariant: The unread data lies in _buf4[_i:_size], and every copied character advances _i exactly once.
Edge cases: If n is zero, no read4 call occurs. When _i catches _size, the next iteration refills before indexing. A zero refill marks EOF; if only part of a four-character chunk was requested, the remaining characters stay available for the next call.
Complexity: Time is O(n) per call plus constant-sized refill work; space is O(1) for the persistent four-character buffer and three counters.
complexity_reason: The method retains _buf4, _i, and _size across calls and writes at most n characters to buf.

title: Read N Characters Given Read4 II - Call multiple times
approach_name: Keep unread characters between calls
notes:
Task and constraints: Provide read(buf,n) for repeated requests over a stream, keeping unused read4 characters available for later invocations.
Idea: Fields buf4, i, and size persist between calls. read refills buf4 when i==size, resets i to zero, exits on a zero-sized read, and copies buf4[i++] into buf[total++] until n characters are delivered.
Technique and why it applies: Persistent buffering decouples read4's four-character chunks from caller-requested lengths, so surplus characters are not discarded at method return.
Invariant: At method entry and exit, indices i through size-1 identify the unread characters remaining in buf4.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero without refilling. When i reaches size, a fresh chunk is requested before indexing buf4. If read4 returns zero, the method stops; if the caller asks for fewer characters than remain, the next call resumes at the saved i position.
Complexity: Time is O(n) per call plus amortized refill overhead; extra persistent storage is O(1) for buf4 and its two indices.
complexity_reason: The persistent char array has length four, and i and size track which buffered characters remain.

title: Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
approach_name: Shrink window when third distinct character appears
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest substring containing at most two distinct characters in a string s of length n.
Idea: lengthOfLongestSubstringTwoDistinct extends a window by right, increments counts[ch], and while counts has more than two keys, decrements the character at left, removes zero counts, and advances left. It updates best with right-left+1 after restoring validity.
Technique and why it applies: A sliding window maintains a contiguous candidate and shrinks only when a third distinct character violates the limit.
Invariant: After the while loop, counts describes exactly s[left:right+1] and has at most two distinct keys.
Edge cases: Empty s leaves best at zero. A string with one repeated character never shrinks and returns its full length. When a third character enters, left advances until one character count reaches zero and the distinct-key limit is restored.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because right advances n times and left never moves backward; space is O(1) for a fixed character alphabet with at most two stored keys.
complexity_reason: Each character enters the window once through right and leaves at most once through left; counts holds at most two keys after shrinking.

title: Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
approach_name: Shrink window when third distinct character appears
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a substring of s containing no more than two distinct characters.
Idea: lengthOfLongestSubstringTwoDistinct updates cnt for each right index, then advances left while cnt.size()>2. Each departing character's count is decremented or removed at zero, and best is updated from right-left+1.
Technique and why it applies: The variable-size sliding window grows across valid characters and contracts only until the distinct-character constraint is met again.
Invariant: At the end of each right iteration, cnt contains the frequencies of exactly the current substring s[left..right], with at most two character keys.
Edge cases: Empty input returns best=0. If all characters match, cnt stays size one and the window covers the full string. When a third distinct char appears, the while loop removes old left-side characters until one key disappears; charAt(left++) reads only an existing index.
Complexity: Time is O(n) since each index is advanced by right and left at most once; extra space is O(1) under the fixed character alphabet and two-key window bound.
complexity_reason: The right loop processes n indices while left only advances, and cnt retains at most two character-frequency entries.

title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
approach_name: Switch heads to equalize path lengths
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shared linked-list node by object identity for two acyclic lists, or None when their paths do not intersect; do not modify links.
Idea: getIntersectionNode initializes a and b at headA and headB. Each pointer follows .next, but when it reaches None it switches to the other list's head. The loop stops when a is b and returns that node.
Technique and why it applies: Head switching makes both pointers traverse the combined lengths m+n, aligning their remaining distance to a shared tail without explicitly measuring lengths.
Invariant: After equal numbers of pointer advances, a and b have each traversed one list followed by the other, so any shared node is reached at the same step.
Edge cases: If both heads are None, the loop is skipped and None is returned. Disjoint lists eventually meet at None. Nodes with equal values but different identities do not count as an intersection because the comparison uses `is`.
Complexity: Time is O(m+n) because each pointer traverses at most both lists; space is O(1) for a and b.
complexity_reason: The loop only advances pointers a and b and never allocates or changes a ListNode.

title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
approach_name: Switch heads to equalize path lengths
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the first shared node by identity in two acyclic linked lists, returning null when they have no common tail.
Idea: getIntersectionNode starts ListNode references a=headA and b=headB. Each advances to .next; when a or b is null, that reference is redirected to the opposite head. The while condition ends when the references are identical.
Technique and why it applies: Switching each pointer to the other list after reaching its end equalizes total traversal length, aligning them at the first common node or at null.
Invariant: After each step, a and b have advanced the same number of times through their respective head-switched routes, so shared-tail alignment is preserved.
Edge cases: If both heads are null, the method immediately returns null. Nonintersecting lists meet at null after both routes finish. Two distinct nodes storing the same int value are not equal references, so value comparison would be incorrect here.
Complexity: Time is O(m+n) for the two traversals; auxiliary space is O(1) because only two ListNode references are used.
complexity_reason: Each iteration updates only references a and b; no collection or node mutation is needed.
